title: Roles, Permissions and Authorization Models
learningObjectives: Model users, roles and permissions with relational tables.
Use junction tables to represent many-to-many assignments.
Query the effective permissions assigned through a role.
Distinguish application-level RBAC tables from native DBMS GRANT and REVOKE statements.

understand.concept: Role-based access control assigns permissions to named roles and assigns users to those roles. The effective permissions for a user are derived through these relationships.
understand.whyItMatters: Centralizing permissions in roles is easier to audit and maintain than hard-coding access decisions separately for every user.
understand.analogy: A job title groups the access a staff member needs, rather than granting each door key individually.
understand.analogyLimit: An application role table does not enforce access at the database engine boundary. Native GRANT/REVOKE and role syntax differ by DBMS; SQLite does not implement server-side roles.

explain.narrative:
## RBAC structure
A typical RBAC model contains users, roles, permissions, a user-role junction table and a role-permission junction table. The junction tables represent many-to-many relationships: one user can hold several roles, and one role can be assigned to many users.

## Effective permissions
A permission is effective when it is connected to one of the user's assigned roles. Query this relationship for display or policy evaluation, but enforce the result in a trusted application/service boundary.

## Native database privileges
PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle provide product-specific principals, roles and GRANT/REVOKE features. Syntax and object-level privileges differ. SQLite has no equivalent server-side user/role system; this lesson's runnable SQLite examples model application authorization metadata only.

## Safe design
Use stable IDs, unique role and permission names, foreign keys, auditable assignment changes and a deny-by-default policy. Re-check authorization on every sensitive operation rather than trusting a hidden UI control.

examples.title: Create role and permission catalogues
examples.code: CREATE TABLE sec20_roles (role_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, role_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE); CREATE TABLE sec20_permissions (permission_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, permission_code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);
examples.explanation: Creates lookup tables for roles and permission codes. Unique constraints prevent duplicate names and permission identifiers.

examples.title: Seed roles and permissions
examples.code: INSERT INTO sec20_roles VALUES (1, 'analyst'), (2, 'viewer'); INSERT INTO sec20_permissions VALUES (1, 'report.read'), (2, 'report.export'), (3, 'user.manage');
examples.explanation: Adds two roles and three permission codes. These are application policy labels, not native SQLite privileges.

examples.title: Create user and assignment relationships
examples.code: CREATE TABLE sec20_app_users (user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, login_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE); CREATE TABLE sec20_user_roles (user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sec20_app_users(user_id), role_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sec20_roles(role_id), PRIMARY KEY (user_id, role_id)); CREATE TABLE sec20_role_permissions (role_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sec20_roles(role_id), permission_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sec20_permissions(permission_id), PRIMARY KEY (role_id, permission_id)); INSERT INTO sec20_app_users VALUES (1, 'asha'), (2, 'bilal'); INSERT INTO sec20_user_roles VALUES (1, 1), (2, 2); INSERT INTO sec20_role_permissions VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1);
examples.explanation: Creates composite primary keys to prevent duplicate assignments, then assigns Asha the analyst role, Bilal the viewer role, and maps permissions to roles. Enable SQLite foreign-key enforcement for actual referential checks.

examples.title: List each user's assigned roles
examples.code: SELECT u.login_name, r.role_name FROM sec20_app_users AS u JOIN sec20_user_roles AS ur ON ur.user_id = u.user_id JOIN sec20_roles AS r ON r.role_id = ur.role_id ORDER BY u.login_name;
examples.explanation: Joins the user-role bridge table to display the role assignments. The bridge table supports multiple roles per user without repeating user or role details.

examples.title: Resolve the read permission for each user
examples.code: SELECT u.login_name, p.permission_code FROM sec20_app_users AS u JOIN sec20_user_roles AS ur ON ur.user_id = u.user_id JOIN sec20_role_permissions AS rp ON rp.role_id = ur.role_id JOIN sec20_permissions AS p ON p.permission_id = rp.permission_id WHERE p.permission_code = 'report.read' ORDER BY u.login_name;
examples.explanation: Traverses both junction tables to calculate which users inherit report.read. The application must still check this policy at the protected service boundary; the SELECT itself does not prevent a direct database write.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples in order. Draw the two many-to-many relationships and explain why composite keys prevent duplicate user-role and role-permission assignments.
practise.independentTask: Add a publisher role with report.read and report.publish permissions. Assign it to a user and query all effective permissions. Explain how an administrator would audit and revoke the assignment.
hints: Use junction tables for many-to-many assignments.
Composite primary keys prevent duplicate mappings.
An application policy query is not a substitute for DBMS-enforced privileges.

questions.explanation: RBAC assigns permissions to roles and users to roles.

questions.prompt: Which table models users assigned to many roles?
options: A single text column of role names
A duplicate users table for each role
questions.explanation: The bridge table represents the many-to-many relationship.

questions.prompt: What prevents duplicate user-role assignments in the example?
options: Composite primary key on user_id and role_id
questions.answer: Composite primary key on user_id and role_id
questions.explanation: The composite key enforces uniqueness for each pair.

questions.prompt: Do application RBAC tables enforce SQLite database file permissions?
options: No; they model application policy only
Only when the table is named roles
questions.answer: No; they model application policy only
questions.explanation: SQLite does not enforce server-style database roles from application tables.

questions.prompt: What is GRANT used for in DBMS products that support it?
options: Assigning privileges to a database principal or role
questions.answer: Assigning privileges to a database principal or role
questions.explanation: GRANT gives specified permissions, with syntax varying by engine.
